newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan investors moving into dual-currency samurais.
newsitem.headline: Japan investors moving into dual-currency samurais.

text.p: Japanese private investors, seeking high returns at a time of low interest rates, are showing a huge appetite for dual-currency samurai bonds, and the trend is likely to continue, underwriters said on Tuesday.
With ultra-low interest rates in Japan expected to continue, high-yielding samurai bonds are likely to remain attractive to many private investors.
"The current situation is extraordinary. We have never seen such massive issuance of dual-currency samurai bonds," an official at the Ministry of Finance (MOF) told Reuters.
In the colourful language of the bond market, a samurai is not a traditional Japanese warrior but a bond issued in Japan by a non-Japanese borrower and denominated in yen.

Dual-currency samurais are issued in yen, and interest is paid in yen, but they are redeemed in other currencies, mainly in the Australian dollar, followed by the U.S. dollar and the New Zealand dollar.
MOF statistics show that the total volume of samurais issued from January to June amounted to 1.799 trillion yen ($16.5 billion). Of that, 1.089 trillion yen ($9.9 billion) was dual-currency issues.
The official said that even at peak times in the past, the annual volume had been no higher than around 650 billion yen ($5.96 billion).
The bonds are not subject to Japanese withholding taxes, and therefore offer advantages to Japanese buyers.
"By looking at the figures alone, we can tell how much demand has risen this year. The demand had mainly come from individual investors," the MOF official said.
Underwriters said total foreign bond holdings by private investors had increased sharply in the past year, with investors tending to favour durations of about three years.
Overseas borrowers are also expected to be keen on raising funds through yen-denominated bonds as they can take advantage of lower Japanese interest rates.

"Sentiment has changed. The depreciation of the yen has made it possible for the private investors to invest in dual-currency samurai bonds," said Mikio Sugihara, chief manager in the international finance section at Nomura Securities.
"The point is that even if an investor keeps one million yen ($9,100) in a bank for a year, the investor won't be able to get much of an interest rate return," Sugihara said.
"They have been cautious about pouring funds aggressively into foreign bonds, but such a feeling has diminished since late last year after the yen's decline," Sugihara added.

Nomura lead-managed a record total of 1.046 trillion yen ($9.5 billion) worth of samurai issues from January to the end of August. This already surpasses the previous annual record of 816.5 billion yen ($7.49 billion) set in 1993. The volume amounted 619 billion yen ($5.67 billion) in 1995.

"Private investors have had nowhere to invest, with Japanese stocks also not performing too well. So samurai bonds appeared to be the most attractive instrument for investors," a senior official at a Japanese securities house said.
"The only reasonable place to invest was the samurai market and they were willing to take currency risks," he added.
Some currency dealers said the dual-currency nature of the bonds would weigh on the yen because foreign borrowers were expected to convert the acquired yen into other currencies.

Takao Sakoh, first vice president at Union Bank of Switzerland in Tokyo, said: "Samurai bond buying by individual investors is only a small factor to weigh on the yen, but there has been a greater trend by investors to shift their portfolios out of Japan into higher-yielding instruments." ($1=109 yen)
